final_proof:
**Conventions.** Here $a \le b$. For a continuous $f:\closedint a b\to\C$ and $a\le p\le q\le b$, the complex integral is defined through its real and imaginary parts:
$$\int_p^q f(t)\,dt := \int_p^q \operatorname{Re} f(t)\,dt + i\int_p^q \operatorname{Im} f(t)\,dt,$$
where the integrals on the right are real Riemann integrals. As usual, an integral over a degenerate interval ($p=q$) is $0$.

**Step 1: $u=\operatorname{Re} f$ and $v=\operatorname{Im} f$ are continuous real functions on $[a,b]$.** For all $z,w\in\C$ we have $|\operatorname{Re} z-\operatorname{Re} w|\le|z-w|$ and $|\operatorname{Im} z-\operatorname{Im} w|\le|z-w|$. So if $|f(t)-f(s)|<\varepsilon$ then $|u(t)-u(s)|<\varepsilon$ and $|v(t)-v(s)|<\varepsilon$. Hence continuity of $f$ at any point gives continuity of $u$ and $v$ there. Restricting a continuous function to a closed subinterval keeps it continuous. A continuous real function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable, so $u$ and $v$ are Riemann integrable on $[a,c]$, $[c,b]$ and $[a,b]$. This means all the integrals below exist.

**Step 2 (real lemma).** *Let $g:[a,b]\to\R$ be continuous and $c\in[a,b]$. Then $\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g=\int_a^b g$.*

*Proof.* If $c=a$, then $\int_a^c g=0$ and the identity is trivial. The same holds if $c=b$. So assume $a<c<b$. For a partition $P$ of an interval $J$, let $L(g,P)$ and $U(g,P)$ be the lower and upper Darboux sums of $g$ over $J$. Since $g$ is Riemann integrable on each of $[a,c]$, $[c,b]$, $[a,b]$, on each of these intervals its integral equals both the supremum of lower sums and the infimum of upper sums, taken over all partitions of that interval.

Let $P_1$ be any partition of $[a,c]$ and $P_2$ any partition of $[c,b]$. Then $P=P_1\cup P_2$ is a partition of $[a,b]$ that contains $c$. The subintervals of $P$ are exactly the subintervals of $P_1$ together with those of $P_2$. Each lower (or upper) Darboux sum is a sum over the subintervals of the infimum (or supremum) of $g$ on a subinterval times its length. Therefore
$$L(g,P)=L(g,P_1)+L(g,P_2),\qquad U(g,P)=U(g,P_1)+U(g,P_2).$$
Since $L(g,P)\le\int_a^b g\le U(g,P)$, we get
$$L(g,P_1)+L(g,P_2)\le\int_a^b g\le U(g,P_1)+U(g,P_2)\quad\text{for all partitions }P_1,P_2.$$
$P_1$ and $P_2$ vary independently. Take the supremum of the left inequality over $P_1$, then over $P_2$. This gives $\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g\le\int_a^b g$. Now take the infimum of the right inequality over $P_1$, then over $P_2$. This gives $\int_a^b g\le\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$. Hence equality holds. $\blacksquare$

**Step 3: conclusion.** Apply Step 2 to $g=u$ and to $g=v$; both are continuous by Step 1. Then
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_a^c f(t)\,dt+\int_c^b f(t)\,dt
&=\Big(\int_a^c u+i\int_a^c v\Big)+\Big(\int_c^b u+i\int_c^b v\Big)\\
&=\Big(\int_a^c u+\int_c^b u\Big)+i\Big(\int_a^c v+\int_c^b v\Big)\\
&=\int_a^b u+i\int_a^b v\\
&=\int_a^b f(t)\,dt.
\end{aligned}$$
The first and last equalities are the definition of the complex integral. The second is rearrangement in $\C$. The third is Step 2. This proves
$$\int_a^c f(t)\,dt+\int_c^b f(t)\,dt=\int_a^b f(t)\,dt. \qquad\blacksquare$$
